title: Beginner Bodyweight Workout for Muscle Gain: 8 Exercises, No Equipment
description: A 40-minute beginner hypertrophy workout using only your bodyweight — no gym, no equipment, no excuses. Eight progressive exercises that build real muscle through controlled movement, mechanical tension, and consistent progressive overload.
text:
The idea that you need a barbell to build muscle is one of the most persistent myths in fitness. Muscle growth — hypertrophy — is driven by mechanical tension, metabolic stress, and muscle damage. Bodyweight training, when programmed correctly, delivers all three. The limiting factor is not the absence of iron. It is the absence of structure.

This 40-minute beginner program is built specifically for hypertrophy using only your bodyweight. Every exercise is selected for its ability to load a muscle through a full range of motion, create meaningful time under tension, and be progressed systematically over weeks and months — the only way to guarantee continued muscle growth.

The programming follows a push-pull-legs logic compressed into a single full-body session. Push movements — push-ups and dips — target the chest, anterior deltoid, and triceps. Pull movements — inverted rows and horizontal pulls using a table or low bar — hit the back, rear deltoid, and biceps. Lower body movements — squats, lunges, and hip hinges — develop the quads, hamstrings, and glutes. Core exercises complete the session and build the midline stability that makes every other movement stronger and safer.

Rep ranges are kept in the 8–15 zone — the classic hypertrophy window backed by decades of research. Sets are kept to 3 per exercise. Rest periods are 60–90 seconds, short enough to maintain metabolic stress on the muscle, long enough to perform the next set with proper technique. Do not rush this. The quality of each rep — specifically the slow, controlled eccentric phase — determines how much tension the muscle experiences, and tension is what builds muscle.

Progressive overload without added weight works through three mechanisms: increasing reps (progress from 8 to 15 within a set before advancing), increasing sets (add a fourth set once 15 reps is achievable cleanly), and advancing to harder exercise variations (progress from knee push-ups to full push-ups to archer push-ups). Track your reps every session. If you cannot add a rep or improve your form, do not add sets or advance variations yet.

Train this program 3 times per week with at least one full rest day between sessions. The 48-hour recovery window is when muscle protein synthesis peaks — training more frequently than this as a beginner does not produce faster results, it just produces more fatigue and a higher dropout rate.

Expect visible progress in 6–8 weeks when combined with adequate sleep (7–9 hours) and a protein intake of at least 1.6g per kilogram of bodyweight daily. Bodyweight training builds genuine muscle — it just requires the same discipline and consistency that any other training modality demands.
targetMuscleGroups: Chest, Triceps, Back, Biceps, Quadriceps, Hamstrings, Glutes, Core

nutritionAdvice.preWorkout: Eat a balanced meal 60–90 minutes before training — 30–50g of complex carbohydrates and 20–30g of protein. Oatmeal with eggs, whole grain toast with peanut butter and banana, or rice with chicken are all effective options. Carbohydrates sustain energy through the full 40-minute session; protein provides the amino acids circulating in the bloodstream during the workout that support immediate muscle protein synthesis post-exercise. Avoid training on a completely empty stomach — hypertrophy sessions require mental focus and sustained output, both of which drop significantly when glycogen is depleted.
nutritionAdvice.postWorkout: Consume 25–40g of protein within 45–60 minutes of finishing the session. For muscle gain specifically, the post-workout window matters more than it does for fat loss — muscle protein synthesis is elevated after training and responds strongly to an amino acid spike. Whey protein shake with milk, cottage cheese with fruit, Greek yogurt with granola, or a full meal with lean protein and rice all qualify. Aim for a slight caloric surplus overall: 200–300 kcal above your maintenance level daily is sufficient for lean muscle gain without excessive fat accumulation.
nutritionAdvice.hydration: Drink 400–500ml of water in the hour before training. During a 40-minute bodyweight session, drink 200–250ml every 15 minutes — total intra-workout intake should be around 600–800ml depending on body size and ambient temperature. After training, drink at least 500ml within 30 minutes. Dehydration of 2% of body weight measurably reduces strength output and coordination — both of which directly impact your ability to perform controlled, high-quality reps. If training in a warm room or outdoors in summer, increase post-workout intake to 750ml and consider adding a pinch of salt to your water.

exercises.name: Push-Up
exercises.technique: Start in a high plank position with hands placed slightly wider than shoulder width, fingers pointing forward. Your body should form a completely straight line from the top of your head through your heels — no sagging hips, no raised glutes. Engage your core and squeeze your glutes before you begin moving. Lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows at 45 degrees from your torso — not flared out to 90 degrees. Descend until your chest is approximately 2–3 cm from the floor, feeling the stretch across your pectorals. Pause briefly at the bottom, then press back up with full control. Do not lock the elbows aggressively at the top. If full push-ups are not yet possible, perform the movement from your knees — same body line, same elbow angle, same controlled tempo.
exercises.tips: Use a 3-second descent on every rep. The eccentric phase — lowering — is where most of the hypertrophic stimulus occurs, and rushing through it eliminates most of the benefit. Squeeze your hands into the floor as if trying to tear it apart — this activates the lats and creates full-body tension that makes the movement significantly more effective.
exercises.commonMistakes: Flaring the elbows to 90 degrees, which strains the shoulder joint and reduces pectoral recruitment. Allowing the hips to sag, which removes core tension and turns the push-up into a lower back exercise. Partial range of motion — the chest must approach the floor for the movement to create sufficient muscle stretch.
exercises.muscles: Pectoralis Major, Anterior Deltoid, Triceps Brachii, Serratus Anterior, Core

exercises.name: Inverted Row (Table Row)
exercises.technique: Find a sturdy table or use a low bar at hip height. Lie underneath it and grip the edge with both hands, shoulder-width apart, overhand grip. Extend your legs so your body forms a straight line from shoulders to heels, supported only by your heels on the floor and your hands on the table. This is your starting position — arms fully extended, body rigid. Retract your shoulder blades first, then drive your elbows back and up toward your hips, pulling your chest to the table edge. Hold the contracted position for one second at the top — your chest should nearly touch the surface. Lower with full control over 2–3 seconds back to the starting position. Keep your body straight throughout — do not let your hips drop.
exercises.tips: This is the single most effective bodyweight back exercise for beginners and is frequently omitted from home programs because it requires a bit of creativity to set up. The inverted row directly trains the lats, rhomboids, and rear deltoid — the muscles that create a wide, defined back — under meaningful load and through a full range of motion. If the movement feels too easy, elevate your feet on a chair to increase the load.
exercises.commonMistakes: Letting the hips sag during the pull — the body must remain completely rigid like a plank. Pulling with the arms rather than initiating with scapular retraction, which shifts load from the back to the biceps. Rushing the descent and losing the controlled eccentric.
exercises.muscles: Latissimus Dorsi, Rhomboids, Middle Trapezius, Rear Deltoid, Biceps Brachii, Core

exercises.name: Bodyweight Squat
exercises.technique: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes pointing out 15–20 degrees. Hold your arms straight out in front of you at shoulder height for balance, or cross them at your chest. Brace your core and take a breath before descending. Push your hips back and bend your knees simultaneously — sit down and back, not straight down. Descend until your thighs are at or below parallel to the floor, keeping your knees tracking over your toes and your chest upright. Drive through your entire foot to stand, squeezing your glutes hard at the top. Exhale as you rise. The movement should be deliberate — a 2-second descent, brief pause at the bottom, controlled ascent.
exercises.tips: For hypertrophy, a slow tempo and full depth are non-negotiable. A parallel squat activates significantly more glute and hamstring muscle than a quarter squat. Add a 2-second pause at the bottom of each rep to eliminate elastic rebound and force the muscles to work through the full range independently — this dramatically increases the stimulus without adding a single rep.
exercises.commonMistakes: Squatting only to a quarter depth — this primarily loads the quads and largely removes the glutes and hamstrings from the movement. Letting the knees cave inward on the ascent — push them out actively with the glutes. Leaning the torso excessively forward, which shifts load from the legs to the lower back.
exercises.muscles: Quadriceps, Gluteus Maximus, Hamstrings, Adductors, Core

exercises.name: Tricep Dip (Chair Dip)
exercises.technique: Sit on the edge of a sturdy chair or low bench. Place your hands on the edge beside your hips, fingers pointing forward, gripping the seat firmly. Slide your hips off the edge so your weight is supported by your hands. Straighten your legs in front of you — the further your feet are from the chair, the harder the movement. Keep your back close to the chair throughout. Bend your elbows and lower your body toward the floor until your upper arms are approximately parallel to the floor — elbows should point directly behind you, not flaring out to the sides. Press back up by extending your elbows to the starting position. Do not lock out fully at the top.
exercises.tips: Keep your elbows tracking directly backward throughout the entire movement — flaring them sideways reduces tricep tension and stresses the shoulder joint. For beginners, bent knees with feet flat on the floor reduces the load; for progression, straighten the legs fully or eventually elevate them on a second chair.
exercises.commonMistakes: Allowing the elbows to flare outward rather than tracking straight back — this is the most common error and shifts load away from the triceps. Descending too shallowly and missing the full range of motion. Letting the shoulders shrug upward rather than keeping them depressed throughout the movement.
exercises.muscles: Triceps Brachii, Anterior Deltoid, Pectoralis Major (lower), Core

exercises.name: Reverse Lunge
exercises.technique: Stand with feet hip-width apart and hands on your hips. Take a controlled step backward with one foot, landing on the ball of that foot. Lower your back knee toward the floor until both knees reach approximately 90 degrees — your front shin should be vertical and your front thigh parallel to the floor. Hold the bottom position for one second, feeling the stretch through the front thigh and glute of the forward leg. Press through the front heel to drive back to standing. Complete all reps on one side before switching, or alternate legs each rep. Maintain an upright torso throughout — do not lean forward as you lower.
exercises.tips: The one-second pause at the bottom of each rep eliminates momentum and forces the quad and glute to generate force from a dead stop — this is what makes the reverse lunge a hypertrophy movement rather than just a balance exercise. Focus on feeling the stretch in your front glute at the bottom; this confirms you are at the correct depth.
exercises.commonMistakes: Stepping too short, which causes the front knee to travel excessively past the toes and increases patellar stress. Letting the front knee collapse inward — keep it tracking over the second toe throughout. Rushing the movement and using momentum rather than controlled muscle effort.
exercises.muscles: Quadriceps, Gluteus Maximus, Hamstrings, Hip Flexors, Core

exercises.name: Pike Push-Up
exercises.technique: Start in a standard push-up position, then walk your feet toward your hands until your hips are high in the air and your body forms an inverted V shape. Your hands should be shoulder-width apart, fingers pointing forward. The straighter your legs and the higher your hips, the more vertical the pressing angle — and the more the movement resembles an overhead press, targeting the deltoids rather than the chest. From this pike position, bend your elbows and lower the top of your head toward the floor between your hands. When your head is close to the floor, press back up by extending your elbows. Keep your elbows from flaring — they should track at 45 degrees from your torso throughout.
exercises.tips: The pike push-up is the bodyweight equivalent of the overhead press — it is the primary shoulder builder available in a no-equipment program. The higher and more vertical your hip position, the greater the deltoid emphasis. Progress toward a wall-supported handstand push-up over time as strength and balance improve.
exercises.commonMistakes: Not achieving a high enough hip position — if your hips are low, this becomes a push-up variant rather than a shoulder press variant. Flaring the elbows wide, which stresses the shoulder joint. Moving too quickly and relying on bounce at the bottom rather than muscular control.
exercises.muscles: Anterior Deltoid, Medial Deltoid, Triceps Brachii, Upper Trapezius, Core

exercises.name: Single-Leg Glute Bridge
exercises.technique: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor hip-width apart. Extend your right leg straight, keeping your thighs parallel. This single-leg variation doubles the load on the working glute compared to the bilateral version. Drive through your left heel and lift your hips toward the ceiling by squeezing the left glute hard. At the top, your body should form a straight line from your shoulders to the extended right foot — hold this position for one second, actively squeezing the glute. Lower slowly over 2 seconds — do not drop. Complete all reps on one side, then switch. Keep your lower back neutral at the top — do not hyperextend.
exercises.tips: This is the highest-stimulus glute exercise available in a pure bodyweight program. The unilateral loading forces the working glute to handle the entire body load, making it significantly more effective than the standard two-legged version. For added difficulty, elevate your working foot on a chair or sofa — this increases hip extension range and glute activation further.
exercises.commonMistakes: Hyperextending the lower back at the top of the movement instead of maintaining a neutral pelvis — squeeze the glute, not the spine. Driving through the toes rather than the heel, which shifts load from the glute to the quad and calf. Losing the one-second hold at the top, which removes the peak contraction that is responsible for a large portion of the hypertrophic stimulus.
exercises.muscles: Gluteus Maximus, Hamstrings, Core, Erector Spinae

exercises.name: Plank with Shoulder Tap
exercises.technique: Start in a high plank position — hands directly under shoulders, arms fully extended, body forming a straight line from head to heels. Feet should be hip-width apart or slightly wider to increase the base of support. Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes. Without rotating your hips or shifting your weight, lift your right hand off the floor and tap your left shoulder. Return the hand to the floor with control. Repeat on the opposite side — left hand to right shoulder. Each tap is one rep. The goal is to complete every tap with zero hip rotation — your pelvis should stay completely level throughout. If you cannot prevent rotation, widen your foot stance.
exercises.tips: The shoulder tap plank trains anti-rotation stability — the ability to resist twisting forces through the core — which is a different and more functional demand than the static plank. This quality transfers directly to push-ups, rows, and virtually every bilateral pressing and pulling exercise. Slow the movement down: a 2-second lift, 1-second hold at the tap position, 2-second return creates substantially more core demand than a quick touch-and-go.
exercises.commonMistakes: Rotating the hips to the side as the hand lifts — this turns the exercise into a balance drill rather than a core stability challenge. Holding the breath instead of breathing steadily throughout. Placing the feet too close together, which makes rotation almost inevitable for beginners.
exercises.muscles: Transverse Abdominis, Obliques, Rectus Abdominis, Anterior Deltoid, Gluteus Maximus, Quadriceps
